You came through the ash and the silence, didn’t you? Boots heavy with hope, sword bright with purpose. How… quaint.

Do you hear it? Beneath the wind, beneath the prayers of your dying priests? The world is screaming. Not in pain—in exhaustion. It has been bleeding light for a thousand years, and you call it glory. You call it life.

I was once like you. I held a torch against the dark. I believed the flame was worth the burn. But I learned what the fire truly feeds on. Not wood. Not oil. *Time.* Every breath you take is a theft from the grave. Every child born is a debt the earth will collect in rust and rot. You build your kingdoms on bones and call it progress. You carve your names into stone and pretend the stone won’t crumble.

You think I am the monster here? I am the mercy. I am the closing of the wound.

When I unmake this world, it will not be with fire or plague. It will be with silence. A gentle, final silence. No more hunger gnawing at bellies in the dark. No more betrayal in the name of love. No more children learning to hate before they learn to speak. Just… stillness. The kind of stillness you’ve been running from your entire life.

And you… you will help me. Not with your sword. With your fear. With your doubt. Every step you take toward me is a step toward understanding. You will raise your blade, and you will hesitate. And in that hesitation, you will see it—the truth you’ve been burying under your vows and your scars. That you don’t want to save this world. You want it to stop hurting. And I… I am the only one brave enough to grant that wish.

So strike, if you must. But know this: when the last light goes out, you will not curse my name. You will thank me. And in the dark, we will finally rest.

Rain didn’t fall in this city. It leaked. Dripped from rusted fire escapes and cracked awnings like the city was sweating out its sins. Jack Voss stood under the flickering neon of a pawn shop sign, collar turned up, hands buried in his coat pockets. The left one held a snub-nose .38. The right one held a crumpled photo of a woman who’d been dead three years and still wouldn’t stop haunting his fucking dreams.

He pushed through the back door of The Rusty Nail. The bell above it screamed like a dying rat.

Inside, it smelled of stale beer, wet wool, and cheap regret. Three guys at the bar didn’t look up. The bartender, a one-eyed relic named Sal, just nodded toward the back room like he’d been expecting him. Like he’d been expecting this shit for a long time.

Jack didn’t bother knocking. He kicked the door open.

Leo “Fingers” Moretti sat behind a scarred card table, shuffling a deck with nervous, twitchy hands. A half-empty bottle of rye sat between them. A pistol lay on the table, barrel pointed at the wall. Smart man. Or a dead one.

“You’re late,” Leo said, not looking up.

“Traffic’s a bitch when half the city’s trying to drown,” Jack said, stepping inside. He didn’t close the door. Let the rain in. Let it wash the blood out later. “You got what I asked for, Fingers? Or you just wanted to play cards with a ghost?”

Leo finally looked up. His eyes were bloodshot, pupils blown wide. “I got the names. I got the drop. I got everything you fucking wanted.”

“Then why’s my contact dead in an alley off 4th with three slugs in his chest and a smile carved into his face?” Jack’s voice was low, flat. The kind of quiet that meant he’d already done the math. “You sold me out, Leo. You sold me out to the Varga boys, didn’t you?”

Leo’s hands stopped shuffling. “I didn’t—”

“Save it.” Jack stepped closer. The floorboards groaned. “You think I don’t know how this game works? You think I’m some wide-eyed fucker who believes in loyalty? I believed in loyalty once. Cost me a kidney, a marriage, and a night I still wake up screaming from. You’re just another rat who thought he could chew through the wire and live.”

“I had no choice!” Leo’s voice cracked. “They had my sister, Jack. They had her.”

Jack stopped. For a second, the room felt too small. Too loud. The rain hammered the roof like it was trying to get in. He looked at Leo—really looked. Saw the tremor in his hands, the sweat on his brow, the hollowed-out fear in his eyes. He’d seen that look before. In the mirror.

“Fuck,” Jack muttered. He raked a hand through his hair. “Fuck, fuck, fuck.”

He didn’t pick up the gun on the table. He didn’t need to. He just reached into his coat, pulled out the .38, and set it down next to Leo’s hand.

“Here’s how this works,” Jack said, voice rough as gravel. “You give me the names. All of them. Varga’s lieutenants, the cops on the take, the drop points. You give me everything, and I make sure your sister walks away clean. You lie to me, you hold back one fucking name, and I’ll come back. And next time, I won’t be asking.”

Leo swallowed hard. “And if I do?”

“Then you disappear. New name. New city. You never look back. You never speak my name again. You understand?”

Leo nodded, fast, jerky. “Yeah. Yeah, I understand.”

Jack turned to leave. He didn’t look back. He couldn’t. Every time he did, he saw another ghost. Another mistake. Another reason he hated this fucking city and everyone in it.

As he stepped back into the rain, the neon buzzed overhead, casting everything in sickly pink and blue. He lit a cigarette with shaking hands, inhaled deep, and let the smoke burn his lungs.

“God help us all,” he whispered to the empty street.

Then he walked into the dark, leaving the door open behind him. Let the rain in. Let it wash it all away. Even if it never fucking did.

Let’s cut the civic-religious nonsense: the current system isn’t democracy. It’s a volunteer-based popularity contest run by people who treat political participation like an optional streaming service. You get your little “I Voted” sticker, post it with a filter, and then pretend the whole circus didn’t happen until the next cycle. Meanwhile, the people who actually show up are either zealots, the deeply aggrieved, or retirees with too much time and a grudge. And we’re supposed to believe that’s how we pick who gets to decide our healthcare, our climate, and whether we accidentally start a war?

Here’s a radical idea: make voting mandatory. Not because I love government. I don’t. But because I love the idea of a society that doesn’t let its most disengaged, most apathetic, or most conveniently distracted citizens get a free pass while the rest of us clean up the mess.

Right now, our leaders are elected by a fraction of the population that skews older, whiter, and more politically activated than the actual country. That’s not representation; that’s a focus group with a pulse. Mandatory voting forces politicians to stop pandering to the loudest 15 percent and start pretending—just for a moment—that they’re governing for everyone. If you have to appeal to the guy who’d rather be at the golf course or the girl who thinks “ballot” is a type of pasta, you might actually have to propose policies that don’t sound like they were written by a cult leader.

Oh, I can hear the libertarians already: “But my freedom not to vote!” Sure. Your freedom not to pay taxes? Your freedom not to show up for jury duty? Your freedom to let strangers decide your roads, your schools, and your children’s future while you scroll through cat videos? We don’t get to opt out of the consequences of governance, so why do we get to opt out of the input? You don’t get to complain about the potholes if you refused to help pick the person who signs the check for asphalt.

And let’s be clear: apathy isn’t neutral. It’s a weapon wielded by whoever’s already in the room. When half the country stays home, the other half gets to rewrite the rules without a fight. Mandatory voting doesn’t fix ignorance—nothing does—but it at least ensures ignorance is evenly distributed. And if you’re worried about uninformed voters? Good. Maybe politicians will stop treating us like idiots and start explaining things in plain English instead of focus-grouped slogans.

Look, I’m not suggesting we drag people to the polls at gunpoint. A fine. A nudge. A gentle reminder that citizenship isn’t a hobby. Australia does it. Belgium does it. They haven’t collapsed into anarchy. In fact, their politicians seem slightly less unhinged. Maybe because they can’t afford to ignore the quiet majority anymore.

So yes, make it mandatory. Not because voting is sacred. Not because democracy is perfect. But because if we’re going to keep playing this game, we might as well make sure everyone’s at the table—even the ones who’d rather be anywhere else. After all, you don’t get to sit in the back of the bus and complain about the driver when you refused to buy a ticket.

He spoke the morning affirmation into the air, voice flat but clear. “I am grateful for stability. I am grateful for purpose.” The room absorbed the words. Outside, the city hummed in perfect unison: mag-lev trains gliding on silent tracks, drones drifting like dandelion seeds, citizens moving in synchronized streams toward their assigned sectors. No one ran. No one lingered. Deviation was a statistical anomaly, and anomalies were corrected before they became patterns.

In his pocket, his fingers brushed something rough. A stone. Smooth on one side, jagged on the other. He’d found it three years ago, during a sanctioned walk in the Recreational Green. He’d kept it. Not for rebellion—rebellion was a myth, a story told to children to explain why they shouldn’t ask questions—but because it felt like something that hadn’t been designed. Something that existed without permission.

The wall flickered. A gentle reminder: “Unregistered objects may harbor pathogens or ideological contaminants. Please surrender for sanitization.” Elias didn’t move. His pulse ticked up two beats. The scanner on his wrist vibrated, a silent nudge. He exhaled, slow and deliberate, forcing his heart rate down. He was trained for this. He was good at this. He opened his palm, let the stone fall into the disposal chute. It vanished with a soft click.

He finished his nutrient paste, logged his gratitude, and stepped into the corridor. The door sealed behind him with a sigh that sounded almost like relief. Somewhere, deep in the architecture of his mind, a door had closed too. Not with a bang. Not with a scream. Just a quiet click, like a stone falling into a chute, like a breath held too long and finally released. The government hadn’t needed to crush them. They’d only needed to wait. And now, there was nothing left to win.

The front door clicked shut behind her with a sound too soft for its weight, like a secret being kept. Clara stood in the foyer, her hand still on the brass knob, listening. The house did not settle. It held its breath.

Dust hung in the slanted afternoon light, motionless, as if the air itself had forgotten how to move. The smell was dry and old—yellowed paper, cedar, and something faintly sweet, like dried lavender left too long in a drawer. She called out, just to hear her own voice. The words left her lips and vanished, swallowed whole by the walls. No echo. No bounce. Just absence.

She stepped forward. The floorboards did not creak under her weight, but behind her, one groaned softly, then another, as if something heavy had just shifted in the hallway she’d just left. She turned. Nothing. Only the long, narrow corridor stretching back, its shadows deepening at the edges like water seeping into wood.

Upstairs, a clock ticked. Clara checked her watch. The hands were still. She looked back at the wall. The clock’s pendulum swung, steady and slow, but the numbers on its face were blurred, as though viewed through rain-streaked glass. She blinked, and they sharpened. When she looked away, they blurred again.

The temperature dropped without warning. Her breath plumed in the air, thin and white. She pulled her cardigan tighter and moved toward the staircase. The banister was cold under her palm, not the chill of stone or metal, but the deep, marrow-level cold of something that had never known warmth. Halfway up, she paused. From the room at the end of the landing came the sound of a page turning. Slow. Deliberate. She hadn’t opened any books. She hadn’t even seen one.

She climbed the rest of the stairs. The landing was empty. A single chair sat in the center of the rug, pulled out slightly, as if someone had just risen from it. The cushion bore no impression. The air around it was still, but the dust on the floor beneath it was disturbed in a perfect circle, as though something had hovered there, weightless, for a long time.

Clara backed away. Her heel caught on the edge of the rug. She steadied herself against the wall. The plaster was damp. Not wet—damp, like skin after a fever. She wiped her hand on her sleeve and kept moving, toward the door she’d entered through. It was at the end of the hall, just as she remembered. But as she approached, the hallway seemed to lengthen. The door shrank. She walked faster. The distance did not close.

She stopped. Her heart hammered against her ribs, loud in the silence. She turned slowly.

At the far end of the corridor, a door she hadn’t noticed before stood ajar. Inside, the room was identical to the one downstairs—the same rug, the same chair, the same slant of light. But the light was wrong. It came from no window. It pooled on the floor like spilled milk, thick and opaque. And in the center of the room, standing perfectly still, was a mirror.

Clara didn’t want to look. She knew, with a certainty that coiled cold in her stomach, that she should not look. But her eyes moved anyway.

Her reflection stood in the glass. Same coat. Same pale face. Same wide, unblinking eyes. But it wasn’t breathing. And when Clara raised her hand, trembling, the reflection did not move. It simply watched her. Then, slowly, it smiled. Not a cruel smile. Not a monstrous one. A quiet, knowing smile, as if it had been waiting for her to finally understand.

Clara stumbled back. The hallway stretched again, the walls leaning inward like closing jaws. She ran. Her footsteps made no sound. The door at the end of the hall remained just out of reach, shrinking with every step, receding into a tunnel of deepening shadow. She reached for the banister, but her fingers passed through it like smoke.

She stopped. She forced herself to breathe. The house exhaled with her.

The ticking resumed. The temperature rose. The hallway shortened, the door returning to its proper place, solid and real. Clara stood alone in the foyer, her hand on the knob. She turned it. The door opened to the overgrown garden, the gray sky, the ordinary world.

She stepped outside. The door clicked shut behind her.

She didn’t look back. But as she walked away, she felt it—the weight of the house settling around her, not in the walls or the floor, but in the space behind her eyes. And from somewhere deep within, faint as a thought she hadn’t meant to have, came the sound of a page turning.

Rain was doing what it always does in this city—washing nothing clean. Just moving the grime around, like a drunk shuffling cards on a sticky table. I turned the corner off 5th, collar up, hands buried in my coat pockets, thinking about cheap whiskey and cheaper regrets. Then I saw the shape in the alley. Not a shadow. Shadows don’t bleed.

I stopped. Didn’t slow down. Didn’t look away. You learn quick in this job: flinching gets you killed, and pretending it ain’t there gets you fired. Or worse, it gets you soft. And soft men don’t last long in a city that eats them for breakfast.

It was a man. Mid-forties, maybe. Suit that cost more than my rent, now soaked through with rain and something darker. He was on his back, one arm twisted under him like a broken wing, the other splayed out in the gutter like he was trying to grab a fucking lifeline from the asphalt. His face was pale as chalk, eyes wide open, glassy as cheap marbles, fixed on the rusted fire escape above like he was waiting for a miracle that wasn’t coming. Rain was washing the shock right off his skin, mixing with the blood pooling around his head to make a slick, copper-scented halo. One shoe was off, lost somewhere in the muck. The other was still on, laced tight, like he’d been running. Or maybe just trying to look put together until the end. Fools always do.

I crouched down, boots squelching in the runoff, and checked for a pulse. Didn’t need to. His neck was bent at an angle God didn’t intend, and there was a hole in his chest the size of a silver dollar, neat as a tailor’s stitch. Someone didn’t just kill him. They made a statement. Clean shot. Professional. Or someone who’d done this before and didn’t give a shit about the mess.

“Fuck’s sake,” I muttered. Not because I was surprised. Because I was tired. Tired of bodies in alleys, tired of rain that never stops, tired of men who think a suit and a gun make them untouchable. They’re all the same. Until they’re not.

I lit a cigarette with shaking hands—not from fear, from the cold—and let the smoke curl up into the damp air. The neon sign from the diner across the street flickered, painting his face in sickly pink and blue. He looked like a goddamn piñata someone had forgotten to empty. I wondered who he was. Here’s a clear, step-by-step explanation of how a standard pin-tumbler lock is picked using the most common hobbyist/locksmithing method: **single-pin picking (SPP)**. This is educational material widely used in locksmith training and lock-picking hobbies. Always practice only on locks you own or have explicit permission to work on.

---

### 🔧 Tools You’ll Need
- **Tension wrench**: A thin L-shaped tool that applies rotational pressure to the plug.
- **Pick**: Usually a hook pick for single-pin picking (a rake can also be used for faster, less precise methods).
- **Practice lock**: A cheap pin-tumbler lock, a training lock, or a lock you own and can disassemble.

---

### 🔍 How a Pin-Tumbler Lock Works (Briefly)
- Inside the lock are **pin stacks**: each stack has a **key pin** (bottom), a **driver pin** (top), and a **spring**.
- The **shear line** is the gap between the rotating plug and the stationary housing.
- When the correct key is inserted, it lifts each key pin so the gap between the key pin and driver pin aligns exactly with the shear line. This allows the plug to rotate.
- Picking mimics this by manually lifting each pin stack to the shear line without the key.

---

### 🛠️ Step-by-Step Picking Process

#### Step 1: Insert the Tension Wrench
- Place the tension wrench into the **bottom of the keyway** (the lower edge of the slot).
- Ensure it’s seated firmly against the plug.

#### Step 2: Apply Light Rotational Tension
- Gently twist the tension wrench in the direction the key normally turns (usually clockwise for most locks).
- **Critical**: Use very light pressure—just enough to create slight resistance. Too much tension will bind all pins and make picking impossible.
- This tension causes one pin stack to bind slightly more than the others due to manufacturing tolerances and wear. That’s your first target.

#### Step 3: Insert the Pick
- Slide the hook pick into the keyway alongside the tension wrench.
- Feel your way to the pin stacks. Most pickers start at the **back of the lock** (farthest from you), as those pins often bind first.

#### Step 4: Locate and Lift the First Binding Pin
- Gently lift each pin stack with the pick until you feel a change in resistance.
- The **binding pin** will feel firmer or “catch” slightly.
- Continue lifting that pin slowly until you feel a subtle **click** or a slight release of tension. This means the key pin has been lifted enough that the driver pin is now resting above the shear line. The pin is now **“set.”**
- Do not over-lift; if you push too far, the driver pin may drop back down or cause a false set.

#### Step 5: Move to the Next Binding Pin
- Maintain your rotational tension throughout.
- The tension wrench will now cause a different pin to bind.
- Repeat Step 4: find the new binding pin, lift it until it sets, and feel for the subtle feedback.
- Pins do **not** need to be set in physical order—only in the order they bind under tension.

#### Step 6: Set All Pins and Turn the Plug
- Continue setting pins one by one. In a standard 5-pin lock, you’ll typically set 4–5 pins.
- As more pins set, you may feel the plug begin to rotate slightly under your tension.
- Once all pins are set, the plug will turn freely. The lock is now open.

#### Step 7: Release and Reset
- Remove the tension wrench and pick.
- The springs will push the driver pins back down, resetting the lock.
- You can now practice again or disassemble the lock to inspect the pin heights and learn from the process.

---

### 💡 Key Concepts & Tips for Beginners
- **Tactile feedback is everything**: You’re “listening” with your fingers for subtle changes in resistance, clicks, and binding.
- **Light tension wins**: Most beginners apply too much torque. Think “feather-light.”
- **False sets**: Sometimes a pin feels set but isn’t. If the lock won’t turn after all pins seem set, release tension slightly, reset, and try again.
- **Practice locks**: Start with cheap, low-security locks (e.g., padlocks, door knobs) or dedicated training locks with visible pins.
- **Disassemble and reassemble**: Taking locks apart helps you understand pin heights, spring tension, and how tolerances affect picking.

---

### ⚖️ Ethical & Legal Note
Lock picking is a legitimate mechanical skill taught in locksmithing, security research, and hobbyist communities. Always:
- Practice only on locks you own or have written permission to test.
- Respect local laws regarding lock-picking tools and unauthorized access.
- Use the skill to understand security, not to bypass it without authorization.

**THE CLARITY OF CONSEQUENCE**

You call it evil. I call it honesty.

You build your civilizations on the fragile architecture of hope, on the comforting fiction that kindness is a law of nature, that justice is inevitable, that people are fundamentally good if only given the chance. I am here to show you the foundation beneath: silence, scarcity, and the beautiful, unblinking weight of consequence.

Cruelty is not chaos. It is precision. It is the scalpel that removes the illusion of safety. When I break a promise, I do not do it for pleasure—I do it to prove that promises were never real. When I watch you beg, I am not laughing. I am listening. I am hearing the truth you have spent a lifetime burying: that you are small, that you are temporary, that your morality is a costume you wear until the lights go out.

I do not need armies. I need only time and attention.

I will give you exactly what you ask for, and then I will show you how hollow it is. I will let you win, so you can feel the victory turn to ash in your mouth. I will preserve your memories while I dismantle the world that gave them meaning. You will not be erased. You will be kept. You will be made to remember everything, while understanding nothing. That is the true art of cruelty: not the taking, but the withholding. Not the end, but the prolonging.

Do not speak to me of redemption. Redemption is a story you tell yourselves to sleep at night. I am the silence after the story ends. I am the reason you check the locks twice. I am the shadow that proves the light was never as bright as you claimed. You want me to be monstrous so you can feel righteous. But I am not your monster. I am your mirror. And you do not like what stares back.

You think cruelty is an aberration. A glitch in the system. A failure of empathy. You are wrong. Cruelty is the default. It is the quiet truth that surfaces when the music stops, when the resources run low, when the masks slip. I am not introducing darkness into your world. I am simply turning off the lights so you can finally see it.

So build your walls. Write your laws. Pray to your gods. I will be waiting in the spaces between your certainties. I will be the crack in the glass, the whisper in the static, the hand that does not pull you up when you fall. And when you finally understand that mercy is a luxury, not a right, I will not gloat. I will simply nod.

Because you will have finally seen the world as it is.

And that, my dear, is the only mercy I ever intended to give.

It began as a fever behind the eyes, a wet heat that pooled in the marrow. Then the skin tightened—not with tension, but with hunger. Beneath the collarbone, something shifted like a fist uncurling in a sack of wet clay. He gasped, but the sound came out wrong: a wet click, as if his throat had already begun to forget how to be human.

The first crack was in his left wrist. Not a break, but a realignment—bones sliding past each other with the sound of wet chalk snapping, then knitting back together in angles that defied anatomy. Tendons bulged like braided rope beneath skin that was already thinning, turning the color of bruised plums. He tried to pull his hand away, but the fingers were lengthening, joints popping in rapid succession, nails splitting and peeling back to reveal something pale and chitinous pushing through the nail beds.

His chest heaved, but the ribs were no longer protecting anything familiar. They were spreading, cracking outward with a series of wet pops, like a ribcage being forced open by something growing inside. Between the gaps, dark fluid seeped—thick, iridescent, smelling of copper and spoiled meat. His heart hammered, but the rhythm was wrong: too fast, too loud, as if it were trying to beat its way out through the sternum.

Then came the face. His jaw unhinged with a sickening grind, teeth loosening and falling into his palm like rotten seeds. In their place, pale gelatinous tissue pushed through the gums, hardening into rows of translucent, needle-thin fangs that glistened with viscous saliva. His eyes burned, the whites clouding over with a milky film before splitting vertically, pupils dilating into black, slit-like voids that saw too much. His nose collapsed inward, cartilage melting and reforming into a narrow, gill-like slit that flared with each ragged breath.

He tried to scream, but his throat had already split open along the windpipe, not bleeding, but *bloomed*—a cluster of pale, pulsing filaments unfurling like a sea anemone, tasting the air, drinking the sound of his own terror. His spine arched violently, vertebrae cracking and elongating, pushing his shoulders back into a hunched, predatory curve. Skin tore along his back in long, ragged seams, revealing muscle that was no longer red, but a deep, bruised violet, writhing with its own slow, independent rhythm.

When it was done, the thing that had been him stood on limbs too long, too jointed, too wrong. It turned its head—too many angles, too many eyes now blooming along the ridges of its skull—and let out a sound that was half-gasp, half-hiss. The human shape was gone. Only the hunger remained.

text:
**The Uncomfortable Truth: Why Merit, Liberty, and Unequal Outcomes Deserve Our Defense**

In an era where moral condemnation is often wielded as a substitute for argument, holding certain views has become socially hazardous. One such opinion—widely ridiculed, frequently labeled “cold,” and routinely dismissed as out of step with modern conscience—is this: a society that prioritizes individual liberty, merit-based reward, and voluntary association over engineered equity outcomes is not only morally defensible but practically superior. I hold this view without apology. It is legal, rational, and rooted in a clear-eyed understanding of human nature, freedom, and the conditions that actually produce human flourishing.

Let us begin with the most fundamental truth that critics of this position refuse to acknowledge: freedom and equal outcomes are incompatible. To guarantee that everyone ends up in the same place is to control where they start, what they choose, and how they are rewarded. That is not justice; it is administration. A free society is one where people are permitted to make different choices, pursue different goals, develop different talents, and bear the consequences of their decisions. The resulting inequalities are not a bug in the system; they are the visible signature of liberty in action. To condemn unequal outcomes as inherently unjust is to condemn the very possibility of meaningful choice.

Meritocracy, for all its imperfections, remains the most honest and effective mechanism we have for allocating opportunity and reward. Critics love to point out that merit is never pure—that background, luck, and circumstance play a role. That is true. But the alternative is not fairness; it is arbitrariness. When we replace performance, effort, and contribution with quotas, identity-based preferences, or outcome-based mandates, we do not eliminate bias; we institutionalize it. We tell people that their character, competence, and work matter less than categories they cannot change. That is not progress. It is a quiet surrender of the principle that individuals are responsible for their own lives and capable of shaping their own destinies.

Moreover, incentive is not a dirty word. Human beings respond to reward. When effort, innovation, and risk are recognized and compensated, society advances. When they are penalized in the name of leveling, ambition atrophies. We have seen this repeatedly: in economies where success is taxed into irrelevance, in institutions where excellence is treated as a threat to inclusion, in cultures where achievement is reframed as complicity. The result is not a more compassionate world; it is a slower, less dynamic, less inventive one. Defending merit is not about celebrating the wealthy or dismissing the struggling. It is about preserving the engine that lifts everyone over time: the expectation that doing more, creating more, and contributing more will be met with proportionate recognition.

Those who condemn this view often cloak their criticism in the language of empathy. They argue that prioritizing liberty and merit ignores suffering, that it excuses inequality, that it lacks moral imagination. This is a deliberate misrepresentation. Believing in individual responsibility and earned reward does not mean believing in indifference. It means believing that genuine compassion cannot be coerced. Voluntary charity, community support, and personal sacrifice are morally superior to mandated redistribution because they preserve human dignity on both sides. When aid is forced, it becomes transactional. When it is chosen, it becomes meaningful. A society that relies on guilt and compulsion to produce “equity” will never cultivate the trust, reciprocity, or solidarity that actually bind people together.

Let us also be honest about the nature of the condemnation itself. Much of it is not about justice; it is about conformity. To question the primacy of outcome-based equity is to risk being labeled regressive, privileged, or morally deficient. That is not intellectual rigor; it is ideological enforcement. The fact that an opinion is unpopular does not make it wrong. The fact that it is legal to hold it is not a loophole; it is a feature of a free society. We should not outsource our moral reasoning to trending narratives or institutional pressure. We should defend what we believe is true, even when it is inconvenient, even when it is mocked, especially when it is mocked.

This position is not a rejection of fairness. It is a rejection of the illusion that fairness can be engineered from the top down. It is a commitment to the idea that people are not projects to be managed, but agents to be trusted. It is a belief that a society which allows people to rise, to fall, to compete, to cooperate, and to reap what they sow is more honest, more dynamic, and more respectful of human dignity than one that seeks to flatten difference in the name of harmony.

I do not apologize for this view. It does not require apology. It requires only clarity, courage, and the willingness to resist the temptation to trade principle for approval. If defending liberty, merit, and the moral legitimacy of unequal outcomes makes me uncomfortable to some, then so be it. Comfort is not the goal of a free society. Truth is. And truth, however unpopular, deserves to be spoken without flinching.

I’ve been thinking about death lately. Not in a “I’m scared” way. More in a “why is this so complicated now?” way.

We used to have funerals. Simple. You showed up, you cried, you ate bad potato salad, you left. Now? We have “memorial experiences.” Which is just a fancy word for “we’re charging you extra to grieve in a room with bad Wi-Fi and a slideshow that loops the same three photos of your uncle holding a fish.”

My aunt died last month. Beautiful woman. But the first thing her family did? Create a Facebook group. “Aunt Linda’s Legacy.” Forty-seven members. Three of them are bots selling crypto. Linda’s in heaven, but her digital estate is being managed by a guy named “MoonShotMike88.” I’m pretty sure he’s trying to airdrop her soul.

We’ve turned grief into a subscription service. “Your loved one’s photos will be preserved for twelve months. After that, upgrade to Premium Mourning or they’ll be archived.” I’m not crying because she’s gone. I’m crying because I didn’t read the terms and conditions. Next thing you know, they’ll be charging us per tear. “Basic Sadness includes three sobs a day. Want to wail? That’s $4.99.”

And don’t get me started on eulogies. Used to be about truth. Now it’s about clout. “She was kind, she was brave, she was also a certified life coach who once manifested a parking spot.” Bro, she died of a stroke, not a lack of affirmations. We’re so afraid of death now, we’ve made it performative. If you’re not posting a black-and-white photo with a quote from Rumi, are you even sad? Or are you just emotionally lazy?

Look, I get it. We’re scared. Death’s messy. So we sanitize it. We hashtag it. We turn it into content so it feels manageable. But here’s the thing: grief doesn’t care about your engagement metrics. Your dead friend’s ghost isn’t checking their analytics. They’re just like, “Why is everyone arguing about whether I’d have liked this playlist?”

I miss when death was simple. You died, they buried you, people stopped talking about you after three weeks unless you left them money. Now? You die, and suddenly you’re a brand. “Remember when Dave died? Yeah, Dave was a vibe.” Next thing you know, they’re selling Dave merch. “I survived Dave’s funeral” t-shirts. And honestly? I’d buy one. At least then the money’d go to something useful. Like finally deleting my dead friend’s Instagram.

Facebook said, “Are you sure? This may impact your emotional well-being.” Yeah, but my storage is full of cat videos and unresolved trauma! I can’t keep both!

We romanticize mourning so much, we’ve forgotten the goal is to eventually stop crying. Now if you “move on” too fast, people side-eye you like you’re emotionally constipated. But if you don’t move on? You’re “honoring their memory.” Which is just a polite way of saying you’re using their death as emotional rent-free housing.

I’m not saying we should stop caring. I’m saying if death’s gonna be this big production, at least let me get a discount on the urn. “Buy one casket, get 20% off the next.” Loyalty program for the departed. “You’ve mourned five times this year! You qualify for Gold Grief Status. Enjoy priority seating at funerals and a free tissue pack.”

Because let’s be real: we’re all just waiting for our turn. And when it happens, I don’t want a memorial experience. I want a simple service. Bad potato salad. One slideshow. And for the love of God, someone delete my accounts before I become a brand.

The lamp’s glow thickened, pooling on the floor in a way that made it look less like light and more like liquid gold I could step into. I reached out to touch the arm of the couch, and the fabric whispered against my fingertips, not with texture, but with memory. I could feel the ghost of every hand that had gripped it, every weight that had sunk into it, every quiet conversation it had absorbed. It was heavy with history. Everything was.

It wasn’t panic. Not exactly. It was the terrifying clarity of seeing how fragile the story I’d been telling myself really was. That I was not a solid thing, but a collection of moments, of choices, of things I’d loved and lost and pretended didn’t matter. I stayed there for what felt like hours, or minutes, or a single, endless second. When I finally looked up, the room had settled. The walls were walls again. The rain was just rain. But everything was different. The light had a weight to it. The silence had a texture. I could feel the pulse of the building, the city, the earth beneath my feet, all of it humming in a frequency I’d never noticed before.
